title: Fortitude (ST II-II.123)
hookLine: courage is mostly endurance, not attack

lines: THE PLASTIC CHAIR, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.
cards: Two kinds of brave. The first runs into the burning building. It's sudden, loud, and it makes the evening news.
The second sits in a plastic chair beside a hospital bed through a long night, and the next, and the next. Nobody films it. There's nothing to charge at, only staying.
Ask the evening news which one is courage, and the first one wins. Ask Thomas Aquinas, and you get a different answer. After prudence and justice comes the third of the cardinal virtues.

teach.b: Fortitude, for Thomas, keeps a person steady in the good when fear pushes them to quit. It deals with two things: fear, which makes us want to run, and daring, which can make us reckless.
Fortitude holds the line between them. Then his surprising claim.
Its main act isn't attacking. It's enduring: standing firm. His reasons: when you attack, you're usually the stronger one in that moment; when you endure, something stronger is pressing on you.
Attack looks to a danger still ahead; endurance faces one already here. And attack can be over in a flash, while endurance has to last.
So staying is often harder than charging. The plastic chair, not the burning building.
Thomas has in mind above all the gravest dangers, standing firm even before death, and he calls martyrdom the highest act of this virtue.
The Catechism describes fortitude more broadly, as firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good.
That widens it to ordinary life: the long illness, the job you can't leave yet, the child who isn't sleeping, the grief that won't hurry.

teach.h: HE THAT SHALL PERSEVERE UNTO THE END.
teach.b: Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved." Persevere. Not win.
Last. And fortitude isn't the absence of fear. Thomas assumes the fear is there; that's what the virtue is for.
A person with fortitude feels the full weight, and doesn't put down the good thing they're carrying.

how: Catholic teaching counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and Catholics honor the martyrs as its highest witnesses while also praying for strength in illness, grief and ordinary trials.

o: boldly charging at whatever threatens you
never feeling afraid of any danger
steadiness in the good, mostly by enduring

s: for Thomas, the main act of courage is attacking
he says the main act of fortitude is enduring: standing firm when something stronger presses.
Thomas thinks enduring is harder than attacking
the one who endures faces something stronger, already present, for a long time.
Thomas assumes the fear is there. the virtue keeps a person steady in the good despite it.

games.q: you're facing something hard that won't be fixed today: a long illness in the family. what does Thomas call the main act of fortitude here?
o: charge at it and force it to end.
endure: stand firm and stay steady in the good.
get away from it as fast as possible.
games.why: Thomas says fortitude's chief act is endurance, not attack, because staying under pressure is harder than charging.

practice: Name one hard thing you're carrying that won't be fixed today, a worry, a body that hurts, a season lasting too long, and breathe beside it the way someone sits beside a hospital bed, letting the urge to run into distraction or anger come, and staying anyway.
If you pray, ask God for strength for today only.

wordCard.voice: Fortitude. For Thomas, the steadiness to hold to the good in the face of fear, whose main act is enduring, not attacking. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: strength, firmness of mind in the face of danger.

carryVoice: Your line: endure. Not fearless, but faithful, carrying the good thing under its full weight. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.
